title: 2 Samuel 19:24–39
context: Mephibosheth, Jonathan’s lame son, meets the king unwashed and ungroomed, and claims that his servant Ziba deceived and slandered him; Ziba had earlier told David that Mephibosheth stayed behind hoping to regain Saul’s kingdom (2 Samuel 16:3–4). David does not decide between them but orders the land divided, and the narrative leaves it uncertain whose account is true, though Mephibosheth’s mourning and his answer in verse 30 are commonly read in his favor. Barzillai the Gileadite, who had supplied David at Mahanaim (2 Samuel 17:27–29), escorts the king to the Jordan but declines a place at court because of his age, sending Chimham in his place. Arminian and Reformed readers commonly treat these encounters as shared ground about loyalty, gratitude, contentment, and the limits of human judgment. The Hebrew of verse 31 has an awkward phrase about the Jordan that translations smooth in different ways, without changing the sense.

verses.text: Mephibosheth the son of Saul came down to meet the king; and he had neither groomed his feet, nor trimmed his beard, nor washed his clothes, from the day the king departed until the day he came home in peace.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Mephibosheth meeting the king unwashed and ungroomed, having mourned since David left. His appearance suggests grief and loyalty.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the description as evidence in his favor, though the narrative does not settle the question. Readers in both traditions commonly read the detail as significant.

verses.text: When he had come to Jerusalem to meet the king, the king said to him, “Why didn’t you go with me, Mephibosheth?”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see David asking Mephibosheth why he did not go with him. The question seeks the truth after the conflicting reports David has heard.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the question as fair given Ziba’s earlier report (2 Samuel 16:3). Both traditions commonly see the king trying to discern loyalty.

verses.text: He answered, “My lord, O king, my servant deceived me. For your servant said, ‘I will saddle a donkey for myself, that I may ride on it and go with the king,’ because your servant is lame.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Mephibosheth explaining that his servant deceived him, since he is lame and needed help to go. He offers a plausible account.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the explanation as consistent with his lameness (2 Samuel 4:4). Readers in both traditions commonly note that this account and Ziba’s cannot both be fully true.

verses.text: He has slandered your servant to my lord the king, but my lord the king is as an angel of God. Therefore do what is good in your eyes.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Mephibosheth accusing Ziba of slander and trusting the king’s judgment, likening him to an angel of God. He submits to David’s decision.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see his trust in the king’s discernment as humble and respectful. Both traditions commonly read the verse as a picture of committing one’s cause to a higher judge.

verses.text: For all my father’s house were but dead men before my lord the king; yet you set your servant among those who ate at your own table. What right therefore have I yet that I should appeal any more to the king?”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Mephibosheth acknowledging that his family deserved death, yet he was given a place at the king’s table. Gratitude marks his words (compare 2 Samuel 9:7).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see his words as recognizing undeserved kindness, a theme some readers in both traditions connect with grace. Readers in both traditions commonly hold that connection as an application rather than the main point.

verses.text: The king said to him, “Why do you speak any more of your matters? I say, you and Ziba divide the land.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see David cutting short the matter and ordering the land divided between Mephibosheth and Ziba. He seems unwilling to decide fully.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the decision as a compromise in a difficult case. Both traditions commonly note that the narrative leaves it uncertain whether David judged rightly (compare Proverbs 18:17).

verses.text: Mephibosheth said to the king, “Yes, let him take all, because my lord the king has come in peace to his own house.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Mephibosheth telling Ziba to take all, since the king has returned in peace. His joy in the king outweighs his concern for property.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see his response as commonly read in his favor, showing loyalty over gain. Readers in both traditions commonly see the verse as a striking contrast to self-interest.

verses.text: Barzillai the Gileadite came down from Rogelim; and he went over the Jordan with the king to conduct him over the Jordan.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Barzillai coming down from Rogelim to escort the king over the Jordan. Loyalty is shown in practical action.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Barzillai’s presence as honoring the one who helped David in his need. Both traditions commonly read the verse as introducing a model of faithful friendship.

verses.text: Now Barzillai was a very aged man, even eighty years old. He had provided the king with sustenance while he stayed at Mahanaim, for he was a very great man.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that Barzillai was eighty years old and had provided for David at Mahanaim. His generosity was costly and timely (compare 2 Samuel 17:27–29).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see his provision as God’s care for David through faithful friends. Readers in both traditions commonly honor his age and generosity.

verses.text: The king said to Barzillai, “Come over with me, and I will sustain you with me in Jerusalem.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see David inviting Barzillai to live with him in Jerusalem. The king seeks to repay kindness shown to him in his time of need.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the invitation as gratitude for faithful service. Both traditions commonly read the verse as a fitting response to loyalty.

verses.text: Barzillai said to the king, “How many are the days of the years of my life, that I should go up with the king to Jerusalem?
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Barzillai asking how many days remain for him, suggesting the move is not worth it. He is realistic about his age.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see his question as wisdom about the brevity of life (compare Psalm 90:10). Readers in both traditions commonly read it as contentment rather than ingratitude.

verses.text: I am eighty years old, today. Can I discern between good and bad? Can your servant taste what I eat or what I drink? Can I hear the voice of singing men and singing women any more? Why then should your servant be a burden to my lord the king?
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Barzillai describing the limits of age: dulled taste, hearing, and discernment. He does not want to be a burden.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see his candor as humble self-knowledge. Both traditions commonly read the verse as a gentle reflection on aging and the value of contentment.

verses.text: Your servant will just go over the Jordan with the king. Why should the king repay me with such a reward?
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Barzillai offering only to cross the Jordan with the king, asking why he should be so rewarded. He serves without seeking reward.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see his modesty as a mark of humble service. Readers in both traditions commonly hold him up as a model of quiet faithfulness.

verses.text: Please let your servant turn back again, that I may die in my own city, by the grave of my father and my mother. But behold, your servant Chimham; let him go over with my lord the king; and do to him what shall seem good to you.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Barzillai asking to die in his own city by his parents’ grave and offering Chimham instead. He blesses the next generation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see his request as contentment with God’s providence. Both traditions commonly read the verse as a picture of a life lived well.

verses.text: The king answered, “Chimham shall go over with me, and I will do to him that which shall seem good to you. Whatever you request of me, that I will do for you.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see David agreeing to take Chimham and to grant Barzillai’s requests. Kindness flows to the next generation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the promise as gratitude carried forward, later reflected in David’s charge concerning Barzillai’s sons (1 Kings 2:7). Readers in both traditions commonly see faithfulness honored.

verses.text: All the people went over the Jordan, and the king went over. Then the king kissed Barzillai and blessed him; and he returned to his own place.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the people crossing the Jordan and David kissing and blessing Barzillai before he returns home. A loyal friendship ends with blessing.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the parting as a fitting close to a story of faithful kindness. Both traditions commonly read the verse as tender and honorable.
